chunks: Measuring R, C, L and impedance. The question: How do I measure resistance/capacitance/inductance/impedance?
You cannot read a resistance, capacitance or inductance directly. You apply a known stimulus to the part, measure how it responds, and calculate the value.
For resistance, push a small current and measure the voltage.
For capacitors and inductors, use an LCR meter, which applies a small AC signal, or build a simple circuit and use a scope.
Real parts change with frequency and DC voltage, so test them near real use.
Suppose you must find the size of a mystery bucket. Pour water in at a known rate and time how long it takes to fill.
A capacitor works the same way: charge it through a known resistor and time the climb. One difference: a real capacitor's value also shifts with the voltage across it.
unknown capacitor charged through a known resistor from a square wave. The scope on V C shows an exponential; tau is the time to reach 63. 2 % of the step.
Resistance: how hard a part makes it for current to flow, in ohms. Capacitance: how much charge a part stores per volt.
Inductance : how strongly a coil resists changes in current. LCR meter: an instrument that applies an AC test signal and reports the part's value, plus how lossy it is.
Four-wire measurement: separate leads for current and for sensing the voltage, so lead resistance does not add error.
Time constant ( tau ): for a resistor and capacitor together, tau equals R times C . It is the time to reach about 63% of the final voltage.
You have an unknown capacitor. Connect it in a line with a known 10 kilohms resistor and drive the pair with a slow square wave.
On a scope, the capacitor voltage reaches 63% of its final value after 1. 0 milliseconds. That time is the time constant, so C equals tau over R equals 0.
001 over 10 000 equals 100 nanofarads. For a tiny resistance like 0. 1 ohms, ordinary leads that add 0. 2 ohms would triple the reading. Four-wire mode avoids that.
That is the whole idea.
"Resistance with a DMM, using four-wire mode for small values and measuring out of circuit.
Capacitance and inductance with an LCR meter at a test frequency near use, which reports the value plus D, Q or ESR.
Without one, a capacitor in an RC with a known R gives C from the time constant on a scope, and an inductor with a known C gives L from the resonant frequency.
For impedance across frequency, including self-resonance and ESR, I'd use an impedance analyzer or a VNA."
